title: US Economic Resilience Comes from Consumers Borrowing from the Future
dek: Barkin explains why consumption stays strong despite high prices: consumers cut savings, skip bills, and delay loan payments to keep spending; AI investment is more about price hikes and crowding out than productivity gains; the Fed may face a long headwind.
why: Micro evidence from the Fed official's frontline: consumers sustain spending by borrowing from the future, AI construction crowds out traditional building, and tariff refunds boost profits. Useful for calibrating views on US inflation stickiness and AI capex.
who: Investors, macro traders, and Fed watchers who want to understand how US consumer resilience and AI investment affect inflation and rate outlook.
skip: You can skip the last two minutes of program promotion and Mount Airy chitchat; Barkin's main content has no repetition.

points.h: You can't get forward guidance from someone who doesn't give it
points.body: Asked about Warsh's Jackson Hole speech, Barkin said he listened carefully but explicitly refused to infer September FOMC action from it. "He doesn't like forward guidance, so you shouldn't look for forward guidance from someone who doesn't give it." Barkin stressed that you can discuss the economy, but if you choose not to give forward guidance, you don't. This also addresses the market's tendency to parse every Fed comment for rate path clues. He described the urge as "we can't help but want to know," but believes it should be restrained.

points.h: Consumers are borrowing from the future
points.body: Barkin's observation: unlike the Great Recession, during the pandemic people accumulated lots of cash, stocks, and home equity, and developed a "I'm going to spend" mentality. Crucially, lower-income consumers are also "creatively finding money": switching to Walmart and dollar stores, cutting insurance, having kids move back home, not paying summer gas bills, and letting auto loans run 60 days past due instead of 120—essentially "borrowing from the future." His conclusion: as long as employment and asset markets are healthy, spending sustained by lower savings and missed bills will continue. This micro mechanism explains the economy's "resilience" better than macro data.

points.h: Data centers crowd out ordinary construction
points.body: In early 2025, $700 billion of investment was announced in a week; transformers, switchgear, and electricians are all in short supply. Barkin believes the construction cycle is shifting from office and multifamily to data centers and industrial. Multifamily "doesn't pencil out" not just because of rates—in 2004-05 rates were similarly high and they were still building a lot. He acknowledges that data center construction does raise costs for other construction, creating a "chicken-and-egg" crowding-out effect, but how much is hard to say. The answer soberly shows the internal disagreement about the spillover of AI capex.

points.h: AI's first impact is on hiring, not output
points.body: At every chamber of commerce and town hall, Barkin hears AI questions that are political: jobs, water, data centers. Economically, AI's productivity shock is still limited to a few replaceable scenarios like call centers, coding, and clerical work; current productivity gains come more from automation and process reengineering driven by the 2022 labor shortage. On the hiring side, employers are already using the logic "can AI do it first, then decide whether to hire" to restrain hiring. The enthusiasm for AI is asymmetric: bosses are active, workers are lukewarm. In other words, AI is affecting the economy by reducing employment demand rather than boosting output.

points.h: Choosing an inflation narrative is choosing a rate path
points.body: Barkin frames today's inflation as two readings. One is "65 months below target, no excuses," corresponding to Warsh's hawkish stance: inflation has been above target for a long time, and rates may not be tight enough. The other is "47 months up and 18 months down": inflation emerged after the pandemic, fell to 2.3%-2.4% by March 2025 after rate hikes, and was pushed back up by AI, tariffs, and oil shocks. He explicitly says the second "is perfectly defensible," and "we will bring it back down later." Which narrative prevails determines whether the Fed keeps tightening or waits for shocks to fade.

points.h: Tariffs are now a stimulus because refunds have arrived
points.body: The tariff topic is quieter than six months ago, not because trade is less important, but because refunds have arrived following the Supreme Court ruling. Barkin says in the past three to four months, companies have received refunds rather than paying extra tariffs. Steel and aluminum producers benefit from tariffs as a "price umbrella"; foreign manufacturers shipping European parts to the US for assembly are hurt by tariffs. Refunds are "very positive" for corporate profits, used for marketing, store renovations, and maintaining hiring, so they have a stimulus effect, but the pass-through to prices is "very targeted," not systemic. This explains why people complain less about tariffs now.

points.h: Data center tax base doesn't buy political support
points.body: Local residents dislike data centers because, unlike factories, there are no workers' kids playing sports with local kids; the tax base benefits touted by economic developers lack political resonance. Barkin jokes that they should name an elementary school after Microsoft or Google to win hearts. He admits he doesn't know how large data centers will become; AI footprint, data center footprint, and energy demand could be significantly under- or overestimated. If political backlash leads to underbuilding, it will drag growth; if overbuilding, it will add to inflation. This is an uncertainty not yet incorporated into the policy framework.

points.h: AI could be inflationary or deflationary; don't bet early
points.body: On whether AI brings a productivity boom and raises the neutral rate R-star, Barkin is cautious. He says the AI path one, two, three years out has an "extremely wide range," could be inflationary or deflationary, with 18 versions in between. Until there is enough confidence, policy cannot be based on assumptions. He also responds to Warsh: different AI model projections point to completely opposite rate directions. Therefore, he implies the Fed should wait for data rather than pre-emptively put AI productivity into the dot plot. This is a warning for those betting on higher R-star.
